title: Family arti
hookLine: a meat-seller teaches a proud scholar that worship starts at home; why arti is a family thing
carry: a householder's home is holy ground
last: TAKING THE LIGHT — WHAT YOU OFFER COMES BACK AS GRACE.

lines: A SCHOLAR, A CRANE, ONE ANGRY LOOK.
I'M NOT A CRANE, YOU KNOW.
cards: A young scholar sits under a tree, reciting the Vedas. A crane on the branch above makes a mess on his head. He glares up in anger, and the bird drops dead.
That's how much power his discipline has given him. Shaken, he goes to beg for food at a house. The woman inside says, wait.
Her husband has just come home tired and hungry, and she feeds him first. When she finally comes out, the scholar is furious. She answers calmly: I'm not a crane, you know.

teach.b: The scholar is Kaushika, and the story is in the Mahabharata. Somehow the woman knows about the bird.
She tells him: if you want to understand dharma, go to the city of Mithila and find a certain man who sells meat in the market. A meat-seller, teaching a scholar? Kaushika goes.
The man looks up from his stall and says: the woman sent you. Then he takes Kaushika home and shows him what he calls his gods: his old mother and father, whom he feeds and cares for every day.
That, he says, is his worship. Then the turn: you left your own parents to study, and they're grieving. Go home.

This is grihastha dharma, the way of the householder. Hindu tradition names stages of life, and many paths honor the one who leaves home for the forest. But this story says the house itself can be holy ground.
Feeding, caring, earning a living honestly: done as dharma, it's worship. That's why evening arti is so often a family thing. It has jobs.
Someone holds the lamp. Someone rings the bell, often the youngest.

teach.h: NO ONE HAS TO. EVERYONE IS ASKED.
teach.b: Everyone sings and takes the light. Real families are complicated. Some people live alone, some with a partner from another faith or none.
Nobody has to join; a guest can simply stand and listen. But the invitation is the point. The meat-seller's temple was a small house with two old people in it.

how: In many Hindu homes, evening arti is a family gathering: one person circles the lamp, a child often rings the bell, everyone sings, and the lamp is passed around so each person can take the light.

o: a festival meal shared after temple worship
arti done together, with a job for everyone
a ritual only the eldest in a house may lead

games.q: the scholar and the meat-seller — tap the pairs.
p: the proud scholar who killed a crane

s: in the story, the wisest teacher is a forest sage
it's a meat-seller in a market town, who cares for his parents at home.
Hindu tradition can treat the home itself as a place of dharma
the householder's daily care, done as dharma, counts as worship.
everyone in the house has to join arti
a guest can simply stand and listen; the invitation is what matters.

games.q: you're Kaushika. the meat-seller has just shown you his old parents. what does he tell you to do next?
o: stay in Mithila and study with him.
go home and care for your own parents.
go deeper into the forest to pray.
games.why: you left your parents to study, he says, and they're grieving. a householder's home is holy ground, and caring for the people in it is worship.

practice: Bring to mind the people you share a roof with, or the ones you'd call family wherever they are. Picture them in the room for arti, one holding the flame, one ringing the bell.
Then pick one person, a roommate, a parent on a video call, a partner, a child, a friend, and think how you might invite them, once, simply, with no pressure at all; if they say no, that's fine too.
If you don't pray, simply picture who you'd want at your table tonight.

wordCard.voice: Family arti: one lamp, one bell, one song, and a job for everyone in the house, the householder's worship done together. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit gṛhastha: the householder, the second of the four stages of life.

carryVoice: Your line: a householder's home is holy ground. The meat-seller's temple was his parents' room. That's day one hundred twenty-two.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana (Aranyaka) Parva: Kaushika, the devoted wife and the Dharmavyadha of Mithila (the 'Vyadha Gita')
The four ashramas (stages of life), with the householder (grihastha) as a full path of dharma
